description: Supine march guide: lift bent knees one at a time lying down to train lower abs, hip flexors and pelvic control, with mistakes and variations.
intro: The supine march is a lying move where you lift one bent knee and lower it, then switch. It trains the lower abdominals to keep the pelvis steady while each leg moves, a skill used in walking and climbing stairs. It is a gentle step up from heel slides.
feel: You should feel your lower belly working quietly and the front of the hip lifting the leg. Your lower back, pelvis and the planted foot stay still. Breathe out as you lift and in as you lower. Watch for breath holding, belly bulging or pushing down into the pelvis. Self-check: hands on your hip bones should not tip as the knee rises.

mistakes.right: Lower slowly and touch down softly. The lowering is where the control comes from.

mistakes.wrong: Arching your lower back as the knee lifts
mistakes.right: Keep your ribs down and lightly draw in the lower belly. Lift less if your back still arches.

mistakes.wrong: Pressing hard into the floor with the other foot
mistakes.right: Keep that foot relaxed. Pushing hard means your glutes and back are taking over.

easier: Lift the foot only an inch, or practice heel slides until the movement feels steady.
harder: Pause with the knee at 90 degrees for 2 to 3 seconds, slow the lowering, or add a gentle Kegel as you lift.
who: People over 50, beginners and anyone who wants a low-impact morning core move.
skip: After abdominal surgery, with a hernia or with separated abdominal muscles, check with your doctor or physiotherapist first. If you notice belly doming, pelvic heaviness or back pain, make the move smaller or rest. Stop if it hurts.

faq.q: What is the difference between a supine march and heel slides?
faq.a: In heel slides the foot stays on the floor. In the supine march it lifts off, so the lower abdominals carry more of the leg's weight.

faq.q: Is the supine march a pelvic floor exercise?
faq.a: It mainly trains the lower abdominals and hip flexors, which work with the pelvic floor to steady the pelvis. You can add a gentle Kegel on each lift, but keep doing Kegels on their own too.
